summary: This document describes the Segment Routing Replication segment, used for multipoint service delivery. It allows a packet to be copied at a replication node and sent to downstream nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: One flyer is photocopied at a stop and sent down several roads, so many people get it from a single original.

questions: what is an sr replication segment
subtitle: A Segment Routing building block that copies one packet at a node and sends the copies to several downstream nodes.

tldr.problem: Multipoint services such as Multicast VPN and Ethernet VPN need one packet delivered to many egress nodes, and Segment Routing had no standard way to say 'copy the packet here and send it on to these nodes'.
tldr.mechanism: A Replication segment is a local segment at a replication node. Its Replication-SID selects a list of replication branches (the Replication state), and the node makes one copy per branch, using a label push for SR-MPLS or the new End.Replicate behavior for SRv6.
tldr.outcome: Replication segments can be used alone, for ingress replication, or stitched into trees by other mechanisms. The document also sets rules for Hop Limit, ICMPv6 errors and ping so replication does not cause error storms.

today: RFC 9524 is a Proposed Standard. It is updated by RFC 9960, so read that document alongside it. It leaves the stitching of Replication segments into trees to other specifications.

sections.title: Introduction and Use Cases
sections.content:
The Replication segment is a new type of segment for Segment Routing (SR). It lets a node, called the replication node, replicate packets to a set of other nodes in an SR domain, called downstream nodes. The RFC specifies the behavior for both SR-MPLS (RFC 8660) and SRv6 (RFC 8986), and it can reach directly connected nodes or farther downstream nodes without state on the transit routers.

The simplest use case is one Replication segment that includes the ingress node of a multipoint service and every egress node as a downstream node. That gives Ingress Replication, which the RFC says is widely used for Multicast VPN (MVPN) and Ethernet VPN (EVPN) bridging of Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, and Multicast (BUM) traffic. Replication segments can also be stitched into trees, but how to do that with a control plane is left to other documents. Managing IP multicast groups, building IP multicast trees and multicast congestion control are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes one message has to reach many places. This document gives the network a way to make copies of a message at a helper stop and send them on.

sections.title: The Replication Segment
sections.content:
A Replication segment is a logical construct, instantiated locally at a replication node, that connects it to a set of downstream nodes. It can be provisioned on the node or programmed by a control plane. It is identified by the tuple <Replication-ID, Node-ID>: the Replication-ID is unique in the context of the replication node (in the simplest case a 32-bit number, with a variable length otherwise), and the Node-ID is the address of the replication node.

The segment holds a Replication-SID (an SR-MPLS label or an SRv6 SID), the downstream nodes, and the Replication state (RS). The RS is a list of branches, and each branch is a <downstream node, downstream Replication-SID> pair. Reaching the downstream node can be given as an interface or next hop, a Flexible Algorithm path, or an explicit SID list or SR Policy.

A packet enters the segment when the active segment is a locally instantiated Replication-SID, or when the root of the service steers it in by local configuration. A leaf has a leaf-role indicator and an empty list of branches. A bud node is both a replication node and a leaf, so it has branches and the leaf indicator. If the segments are stitched by local provisioning, a chain of them SHOULD NOT form a loop, and a control plane MUST prevent loops or detect and mitigate them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper keeps a list that says who to hand a copy to next. If the list is empty, the helper is the last stop and keeps the flyer.

sections.title: The SR-MPLS Data Plane
sections.content:
When the active segment is a Replication-SID, processing is a POP followed by a lookup of the RS. For each branch, the node does a PUSH of the downstream Replication-SID, plus an optional segment list, to steer the copy toward the downstream node. At a leaf or bud node the operation is NEXT, and delivery of the payload off the tree follows local configuration.

SIDs MAY be inserted before the downstream Replication-SID to reach a non-adjacent node. A replication node MAY use an Anycast-SID or a BGP PeerSet-SID to send a copy to one replication node in a set, but only if all nodes in the set have an identical Replication-SID and reach the same set of receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper takes off its own label, looks at its list, and sticks a new label on each copy so the copy goes to the right next helper.

sections.title: SRv6 and the End.Replicate Behavior
sections.content:
For SRv6 the RFC defines End.Replicate, short for 'Endpoint with replication and/or decapsulate'. The RS conceptually holds a Node-Role (Head, Transit, Leaf or Bud), an IPv6 Hop Limit Threshold whose default is zero, and a Replication-List. Each list entry has a downstream node, a downstream Replication-SID and an optional Segment-List.

To replicate, the node copies the packet for each entry and sets the IPv6 Destination Address from local state, not from the SRH. If the Segment-List is not empty, it applies H.Encaps or H.Encaps.Red to steer the copy. The copy then goes to the egress IPv6 FIB lookup. At a leaf or bud node, the node processes the next header. IPv4 (type 4), IPv6 (type 41) and Ethernet (type 143) payloads have the outer IPv6 header removed first; other upper-layer types are processed only if local configuration allows them, and otherwise the packet is discarded.

If a root encodes a context-SID in an SRH with an HMAC TLV, it MUST set the D bit, because the Replication-SID is not part of the SRH segment list. IANA assigned End.Replicate the value 75 (0x004B) in the SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors registry.
sections.plainLanguage: For the IPv6 version, the helper makes a copy, writes the next helper's address on the envelope, and sends it off. The last helper opens the envelope and delivers what is inside.

sections.title: Hop Limit, ICMPv6 Errors and Ping
sections.content:
A replication node MUST decrement the IPv6 Hop Limit, and it must be non-zero for the node to replicate. Nodes that merely forward replicated packets can drop the Hop Limit to zero and send ICMPv6 errors to the root, which could cause a storm. To avoid that, a Replication segment has an optional IPv6 Hop Limit Threshold. If it is set, a replication node MUST discard an incoming packet whose Hop Limit is below it and log this in a rate-limited way. The threshold SHOULD be set so a packet can reach the furthest leaf.

An SRv6 implementation MUST follow the rule in RFC 4443 that no ICMPv6 error is originated for a packet sent to a multicast address, including its two exceptions: Packet Too Big, and Parameter Problem with Code 2 for an unrecognized IPv6 option. For OAM, a source that knows a leaf or bud Replication-SID can ping it directly, or ping it through a transit node's Replication-SID. In that case the Echo Request checksum is computed with the leaf's SID as the destination. Other leaves that receive a copy drop it because of the checksum mismatch. Traceroute to a leaf or bud Replication-SID is not possible, since ICMPv6 Time Exceeded cannot be originated.
sections.plainLanguage: If a copied message gets lost, every helper must not shout back to the sender at once. The rules keep the shouting small and make pinging work in a careful way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new behaviors are meant to run inside an SR domain, which needs protection from outside attackers as described in RFC 8754. For SR-MPLS that means disabling MPLS on external interfaces of edge nodes or filtering labeled traffic. For SRv6 it means dropping packets from outside whose destination is in the SID block with infrastructure ACLs, and denying spoofed source addresses as in BCP 84.

The RFC argues that an attacker who gets past the filters cannot use a stack of Replication segments for amplification or link exhaustion, because trees always end at a leaf or bud node with decapsulation. The attacker can, however, inject traffic to receivers of a P2MP service. Loops from provisioning without a control plane can cause a storm until the MPLS TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit reaches zero. Forged packets that cause many ICMPv6 errors to a victim are mitigated by the Hop Limit Threshold check.
sections.plainLanguage: The network keeps strangers away from the copy machine. Even if someone sneaks in, the copies always end at the last helpers instead of growing forever.

sections.title: Worked Examples in Appendix A
sections.content:
The appendix uses a topology of nodes R1 to R7. A Replication segment is rooted at R1 with downstream nodes R2, R6 and R7, and the copy to R7 has to pass R4. Nodes R3, R4 and R5 have no Replication segment. R2, R6 and R7 are leaves.

In the SR-MPLS example, the copy to R2 is sent directly on interface L12. The copy to R6 carries <N-SID6, R-SID6>. The copy to R7 carries <N-SID4, A-SID47, R-SID7> so it goes through R4. In the SRv6 example, R1 uses H.Encaps.Red with an End.X SID at R4 for the copy to R7, or, as the root, merges the two encapsulations into one.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show one sender with three receivers. Two copies go the short way, and the third is told to stop at a particular helper on the way.
